title: Checks at boundaries, after short films
statement: Break any long film that carries content a student needs with required quick checks, placed only at natural boundaries, and put a short film's check straight after it.
example: The line sits at about 60 seconds: under a minute, a pause is likely to feel like an odd interruption, longer perhaps than the film itself.
detail: One version of the intro-video BrainLift uses checks inside videos over about 60 seconds and puts the check straight after shorter ones (`downloads/BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md`, line 309). Its reason is that a check earns its interruption by landing on a boundary, where it consolidates what was just taught and clears working memory before the next thing arrives (line 311). Its worked 60-second script has no embedded checks (line 363), while a built Grade 3 lesson's 1:54 film pauses twice for a check (`downloads/SUPERSEDED — see v2 (table format)_ WITW Lesson 1 learning walkthrough.md`, line 25). A short film here is one under about a minute.
against: The source calls the rule "a sensible estimate based on experience" (`downloads/BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md`, line 311). A rule for intro films bars any question after the film that asks what happens next, because choosing what to repeat leaks which threads matter; that covers a short preview, not video that carries content. A later run found counter-evidence (`grade3-reading/ui-audit-2026-09-08/feedback-reconciliation/invariants.dom.txt`).
